title: Saddam's Iraq
subtitle: 1979–2003 · Three Wars and a Genocide — the Iran War and the Chemical Weapons, the Anfal and Halabja, Kuwait and the Gulf War, the Crushed Uprisings and the Drained Marshes, the Sanctions Decade, and the Fall

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Saddam absolute, the Iran–Iraq War, Kuwait and the Gulf War, the 1991 uprisings and their crushing, the sanctions state and the Faith Campaign, and the Shia, Kurdish and exile oppositions

entries.label: Saddam absolute
entries.hint: Saddam Hussein took the presidency in July 1979 and, at a filmed party conference, had dozens of 'conspirators' named and led out to be shot. For twenty-four years he ruled without limit — the party, the state and a spreading net of clan and Tikriti loyalists in the security posts, the statues and portraits and palaces, his sons Uday and Qusay as heirs. The machine had been built in the previous decade; now it had one master.
entries.note: Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear' (1989); Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party' (2012).

entries.label: The Iran–Iraq War
entries.hint: In September 1980 Saddam invaded Iran, expecting a quick win over a revolution in chaos. Instead came eight years of trench warfare, missile attacks on cities, Iranian human-wave assaults, and — from 1983 — Iraqi chemical weapons used on a scale not seen since the First World War. Perhaps a million died. Iraq called it a victory and emerged with a huge army, an arsenal, and eighty billion dollars of debt to the Gulf states.
entries.note: Pierre Razoux, 'The Iran–Iraq War' (2015); Efraim Karsh, 'The Iran–Iraq War 1980–1988' (2002).

entries.label: Kuwait and the Gulf War
entries.hint: On 2 August 1990 Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait — over the war debt, the oil price, and a claimed border. The response was a coalition of thirty-five states, a UN authorisation, and the most comprehensive sanctions ever imposed. In January–February 1991 an air campaign and a hundred-hour ground war drove the Iraqi army out with tens of thousands of casualties, and left the regime in place but the country broken.
entries.note: Lawrence Freedman & Efraim Karsh, 'The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991' (1993); Rick Atkinson, 'Crusade' (1993).

entries.label: The 1991 uprisings and their crushing
entries.hint: After the defeat, fifteen of Iraq's eighteen provinces rose — the Shia south and the Kurdish north almost at once. The Republican Guard, spared by the ceasefire, put them down with helicopter gunships as the United States watched from the border: the shrine cities shelled, mass graves filled, perhaps a hundred thousand killed, and two million Kurds driven into the mountains. Out of that flight came the no-fly zones and the Kurdish safe haven.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Endless Torment: The 1991 Uprising in Iraq' (1992); Kanan Makiya, 'Cruelty and Silence' (1993).

entries.label: The sanctions state
entries.hint: Under thirteen years of siege the regime adapted and survived: the ration card that made every Iraqi dependent on the state, the smuggling and the crony enrichment, the Faith Campaign that dressed the Baʿth in religion, the restored tribal shaykhs as instruments of control, and the family feuds — the Kamel brothers' defection and murder in 1995, the attempt on Uday's life in 1996. The apparatus tightened as the country fell apart.
entries.note: Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party' (2012); Amatzia Baram, 'Saddam Husayn and Islam' (2014).

entries.label: The Shia Islamists, in exile and at home
entries.hint: The regime executed Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr in 1980 and drove the Shia opposition abroad: SCIRI and its Badr Corps formed in Tehran in 1982, the Daʿwa in exile from Iran to London. At home, from the mid-1990s, a second ayatollah, Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr, built a mass following among the poor Shia — until he too was murdered, with two sons, in Najaf in 1999. His surviving son Muqtada would inherit the movement.
entries.note: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003); Patrick Cockburn, 'Muqtada' (2008).

entries.label: The Kurdish safe haven and the KRG
entries.hint: Under the umbrella of the no-fly zone the Iraqi Kurds built a de facto state from 1991: an elected parliament, a regional government, their own budget from the customs and later the Oil-for-Food set-aside. It nearly destroyed itself in a KDP–PUK civil war from 1994 to 1998, with Baghdad and Tehran and Ankara all intervening. But it held, and it was the one part of Iraq ready and willing to help the invasion of 2003.
entries.note: Gareth Stansfield, 'Iraqi Kurdistan: Political Development and Emergent Democracy' (2003); David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004).

entries.label: The exiles and the road to Washington
entries.hint: The exile opposition coalesced in 1992 as the Iraqi National Congress under Ahmed Chalabi, and set out to persuade the United States to remove Saddam by force. The 1998 Iraq Liberation Act made regime change American law; the neoconservatives made the case; the containment of a decade had exhausted its patrons. After 11 September 2001 the argument was won, and the invasion followed in March 2003.
entries.note: George Packer, 'The Assassins' Gate' (2005); Aram Roston, 'The Man Who Pushed America to War: The Life of Ahmed Chalabi' (2008).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The eight-year war with Iran and the chemical weapons, the Anfal genocide and Halabja, Desert Storm, the Sha'ban Intifada and the shelled shrines, the draining of the marshes as counter-insurgency, and the 2003 invasion

entries.label: The Iran–Iraq War at the front
entries.hint: After the opening thrust into Khuzestan stalled, the war settled into a First World War landscape of trenches, barbed wire and mass infantry assault along the border. Iraq answered Iran's numbers with poison gas — mustard and, from 1984, the nerve agent tabun — sprayed on Iranian positions and, at Halabja, on a Kurdish town. The Faw peninsula changed hands twice. It ended in 1988 with a ceasefire on the 1980 line and a million dead.
entries.note: Pierre Razoux, 'The Iran–Iraq War' (2015); Joost Hiltermann, 'A Poisonous Affair: America, Iraq, and the Gassing of Halabja' (2007).

entries.label: The Anfal and Halabja
entries.hint: Under Ali Hassan al-Majid the regime ran a campaign of extermination against the rural Kurds — 'al-Anfal', named for a chapter of the Quran. Some four thousand villages were bulldozed, the 'prohibited zones' cleared by execution, and gas used on dozens of targets, killing around five thousand at Halabja in a single attack in March 1988. Between fifty thousand and a hundred and eighty thousand Kurds were killed or disappeared.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch / Middle East Watch, 'Genocide in Iraq: The Anfal Campaign against the Kurds' (1993).

entries.label: Desert Storm
entries.hint: The coalition opened on 17 January 1991 with a five-week air campaign that destroyed Iraq's command, its power grid, its bridges and much of its army from the air. The ground assault on 24 February took a hundred hours: the Iraqi forces in and around Kuwait were routed, the retreat down the road to Basra was strafed into the 'Highway of Death', and the war was halted with the Republican Guard largely intact.
entries.note: Lawrence Freedman & Efraim Karsh, 'The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991' (1993); Michael Gordon & Bernard Trainor, 'The Generals' War' (1995).

entries.label: The Sha'ban Intifada
entries.hint: The uprising began among defeated soldiers in Basra on 1 March 1991 and spread within days across the Shia south and the Kurdish north. For two or three weeks the regime held only Baghdad and its own province. Then the Guard drove south with tanks and gunships: the shrines of Najaf and Karbala were shelled and stormed, prisoners were shot in the streets and buried in pits, and the survivors fled to Iran and Saudi Arabia and the marshes.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Endless Torment: The 1991 Uprising in Iraq and Its Aftermath' (1992).

entries.label: The draining of the marshes
entries.hint: To deny the 1991 rebels their refuge and to break the Maʿdan who sheltered them, the regime built embankments and a network of canals — the 'Third River', the 'Mother of Battles River' — that dried some ninety per cent of the marshes within a decade. A wetland that had existed since the beginning of Sumer, and the last people who lived the old marsh life, were destroyed together. It was ecological warfare on a historic scale.
entries.note: the UNEP report 'The Mesopotamian Marshlands: Demise of an Ecosystem' (2001); Sayyid Nadhir al-Khayyun and the Maʿdan testimony.

entries.label: The 2003 invasion
entries.hint: On 20 March 2003 a United States–led force crossed from Kuwait, drove up the two rivers against crumbling resistance, and reached Baghdad in three weeks. On 9 April the city fell, and a crowd with American help pulled down a statue of Saddam in Firdos Square. The regime evaporated; Saddam went into hiding and was taken from a hole near Tikrit in December. The war was over; the occupation and the wreck were beginning.
entries.note: Michael Gordon & Bernard Trainor, 'Cobra II' (2006); George Packer, 'The Assassins' Gate' (2005).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Total personal rule and the clan, the security state at war, the command economy under sanctions and the ration card, the Faith Campaign and the re-Islamisation of the Ba'th, the re-tribalisation, and the Kurdish region as a separate order

entries.label: Total personal rule
entries.hint: Under Saddam the party, the state, the army and the leader's clan fused into one thing answerable only to him. The key security and command posts went to men of Tikrit and the Bu Nasir kin; the Revolutionary Command Council rubber-stamped; and a cult filled the country with statues, portraits, murals and palaces. His sons Uday, who ran the militias and the media, and Qusay, who ran the security services, were the designated heirs.
entries.note: Joseph Sassoon, 'Saddam Hussein's Baʿth Party: Inside an Authoritarian Regime' (2012); Kevin Woods & others, 'The Saddam Tapes' (2011).

entries.label: The security state at war
entries.hint: The intelligence services — party intelligence, general security, military intelligence, special security, and Saddam's own guard — were turned inward and multiplied for mutual watching. Collective punishment was doctrine: the razing of a rebel's village, the arrest of his family, the execution of whole categories. The 1991 uprisings and the Anfal were this apparatus at full stretch. Fear, as Kanan Makiya wrote, was the state's organising principle.
entries.note: Kanan Makiya, 'Republic of Fear: The Politics of Modern Iraq' (updated edition, 1998); the captured Baʿth documents held at the Hoover Institution.

entries.label: The command economy of scarcity
entries.hint: When sanctions crushed the economy the regime rebuilt control around scarcity. The monthly food ration, distributed through a network of registered agents, kept most Iraqis fed and utterly dependent on the state. A black market and a smuggling economy — through Jordan, Turkey and the Gulf — enriched the regime's cronies. Losing the ration, or the regime's favour, meant destitution. The state was the only source of survival.
entries.note: Sarah Graham-Brown, 'Sanctioning Saddam: The Politics of Intervention in Iraq' (1999); Joy Gordon, 'Invisible War: The United States and the Iraq Sanctions' (2010).

entries.label: The Faith Campaign
entries.hint: From 1993 the secular Baʿth wrapped itself in Islam. 'Allāhu akbar' went onto the flag in Saddam's handwriting; a Quran was said to be written in his blood; mosques rose, the largest named for the Mother of All Battles, its minarets shaped as missile bodies and rifle barrels. Alcohol and nightclubs were banned, thieves' hands amputated, 'honour killing' decriminalised. It was a bid to borrow the legitimacy the regime had lost.
entries.note: Amatzia Baram, 'Saddam Husayn and Islam, 1968–2003' (2014); Ofra Bengio, 'Saddam's Word' (1998).

entries.label: The re-tribalisation
entries.hint: The party that had spent decades trying to break the tribes now restored their shaykhs — as recruiting agents, arms distributors, local enforcers and hostages for their people's good behaviour, paid in land, money, weapons and a licence to run their own 'tribal law'. It was a deliberate reversal, an admission that the Baʿthist state could no longer reach the ground on its own, and it left a militia-ready society for what came after.
entries.note: Amatzia Baram, 'Neo-Tribalism in Iraq: Saddam Hussein's Tribal Policies 1991–96' (1997); Faleh A. Jabar & Hosham Dawod (eds.), 'Tribes and Power' (2003).

entries.label: The Kurdish region governs itself
entries.hint: North of the 36th parallel, out of Baghdad's reach, the Kurds ran their own affairs from 1991: a parliament elected in 1992, a regional government, ministries, a budget from cross-border trade and later a share of Oil-for-Food. Territory and revenue were split between the KDP around Erbil and the PUK around Sulaymaniyya, and the two fought a war over it, but the institutions survived — a proto-state incubating for twelve years.
entries.note: Gareth Stansfield, 'Iraqi Kurdistan: Political Development and Emergent Democracy' (2003).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Faith Campaign from above and the surge of popular religiosity from below, the Shia clergy under the regime and the murder of the Sadrs, the sharpening of sectarian consciousness, and the exile and the diaspora

entries.label: Religion from above and from below
entries.hint: Two things happened at once. The regime Islamised the state from the top down, as policy. And Iraqis, ground down by war and siege, turned to religion from the bottom up: the mosques filled, the veil returned to streets that had abandoned it, the Ashura and the pilgrimage drew crowds where they were tolerated. A society that the Baʿth had spent thirty years secularising was re-Islamising fast, and the two currents did not always align.
entries.note: Amatzia Baram, 'Saddam Husayn and Islam' (2014); Fanar Haddad, 'Sectarianism in Iraq' (2011).

entries.label: The Shia clergy under the regime
entries.hint: The regime tried to break the marjaʿiyya: al-Sadr executed in 1980, Grand Ayatollah al-Khoei detained and humiliated after 1991, Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr and two sons shot in Najaf in 1999. The seminary emptied through emigration and fear. What survived was the quietist, Iranian-born Ali al-Sistani, who kept his head down and his authority intact — and who would step into the vacuum the moment the regime fell.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'Reaching for Power: The Shiʿa in the Modern Arab World' (2006); Patrick Cockburn, 'Muqtada' (2008).

entries.label: Sectarian consciousness sharpened
entries.hint: The regime cast the Iran war as a fight against Persian Shi'ism, the 1991 rising as Shia treachery, and its enemies at home as agents 'of Iranian origin' — and it staffed the security core with Sunni Arabs of the favoured tribes and regions. Under that pressure a defensive Shia identity hardened, and Sunni Iraqis grew used to being the state. The sectarian consciousness that exploded after 2003 was forged in these years, not imported.
entries.note: Fanar Haddad, 'Sectarianism in Iraq: Antagonistic Visions of Unity' (2011).

entries.label: The exile and the diaspora
entries.hint: Between two and four million Iraqis left — doctors, engineers, academics, artists, and whole persecuted communities of Kurds, Shia, Christians and Faili Kurds — for Iran, Jordan, Syria, the Gulf, Europe, North America and Australia. They sent money home and kept a parallel Iraq alive abroad: the political fronts, the presses, the seminaries in Qom and Damascus, the memory. Some would return in 2003 to govern; most would not.
entries.note: Nabil Al-Tikriti and others on the Iraqi diaspora; the UNHCR figures for the period.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The literature of war and exile, the monumental Baghdad of Saddam, the looting and destruction of heritage, the suppressed and the surviving arts, and the information war

entries.label: The literature of war and exile
entries.hint: The regime commissioned a whole literature of the Iran war — heroic poetry, patriotic fiction, a prize named for the Qadisiyya of 636. The real writing was done quietly at home or in exile: the poets Saʿdi Yusuf, Fadhil al-Azzawi, Sargon Boulus abroad; the war and prison memoirs; the fiction that would surface only after 2003. It is a literature of catastrophe, and most of it had to leave the country to be written.
entries.note: muhsin al-Musawi, 'Reading Iraq: Culture and Power in Conflict' (2006); Salaam Yousif on Iraqi war culture.

entries.label: The monumental Baghdad of Saddam
entries.hint: The regime turned Baghdad into a stage set of itself. The Victory Arch of 1989 — two pairs of forty-metre bronze forearms, cast from moulds of Saddam's own, holding crossed swords, with real helmets of dead Iranian soldiers embedded in the pavement beneath. The Mother of All Battles Mosque with minarets like missiles and rifle barrels. A ring of vast palaces. Architecture as the cult in concrete and bronze.
entries.note: Kanan Makiya, 'The Monument: Art, Vulgarity and Responsibility in Iraq' (1991).

entries.label: The looting and rebuilding of heritage
entries.hint: Saddam rebuilt the walls of Babylon on top of the ancient ones, with bricks stamped, in the manner of Nebuchadnezzar, 'built by Saddam Hussein', and put a palace on a mound overlooking the site. The Gulf War and then the sanctions gutted site protection: an epidemic of illegal digging fed a global market in Iraqi antiquities. In April 2003, in the days after the fall, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad was ransacked.
entries.note: Magnus Bernhardsson, 'Reclaiming a Plundered Past' (2005); Lawrence Rothfield, 'The Rape of Mesopotamia' (2009).

entries.label: The suppressed and the surviving arts
entries.hint: Iraq's strong modern-art tradition contracted into a shrinking space: the painters and sculptors who stayed worked for the regime, or in silence, or for a black-market trade in canvases smuggled out through Amman. The serious theatre was reduced to propaganda or shut; the cinema died; the concert halls emptied. The maqam and the old songs survived in the coffee-houses and the cassette. Art was under siege with everything else.
entries.note: Nada Shabout, 'Modern Arab Art' (2007), on the sanctions-era contraction; the Amman gallery trade.

entries.label: The information war
entries.hint: The regime fought its wars in images too — the 'Mother of All Battles' rhetoric, the human-shield broadcasts, the information minister of 2003 announcing victory as the tanks arrived. Satellite dishes were banned and then, quietly, everywhere; Al Jazeera arrived in 1996; the sanctions were argued abroad as 'genocide by numbers' and at home as the enemy's crime. The picture of Iraq was itself a battlefield.
entries.note: Ofra Bengio, 'Saddam's Word: Political Discourse in Iraq' (1998); the coverage studies of the Gulf and 2003 wars.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The making of the case against Iraq, the sanctions debate and the ethics of collective punishment, the Shia political thought in exile, and the documenting of the crimes

entries.label: The making of the case against Iraq
entries.hint: Through the 1990s an argument built in Washington and London for removing Saddam by force: the neoconservative case that a democratic Iraq would transform the region, written into the 1998 Iraq Liberation Act; the humanitarian case made by exiles and by writers like Kanan Makiya; the security case about the weapons; and a weariness with the endless containment. After 11 September 2001 these strands fused into a policy.
entries.note: George Packer, 'The Assassins' Gate: America in Iraq' (2005); Kanan Makiya, 'Cruelty and Silence' (1993).

entries.label: The debate over the sanctions
entries.hint: The sanctions decade became a running argument about the ethics of economic warfare: the UNICEF surveys of child mortality, the resignations of two UN humanitarian coordinators in protest, the 1996 television exchange in which a US official called the deaths of half a million children 'worth it', and the regime's own use of the suffering as a weapon of publicity. It is a defining case in the morality of collective punishment.
entries.note: Joy Gordon, 'Invisible War: The United States and the Iraq Sanctions' (2010); Denis Halliday's and Hans von Sponeck's writings.

entries.label: Shia political thought in exile
entries.hint: In Tehran, Qom, Damascus and London the exiled Shia movements worked out what a post-Saddam Iraq should be: SCIRI drawing on Khomeini's rule of the jurist, the Daʿwa arguing for an elected Islamic state, and — as a counterweight — the emerging quietist line of Sistani, who held that the clergy should guide but not govern. These were the blueprints that the political class of post-2003 Iraq would bring home.
entries.note: Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Shiʿite Movement in Iraq' (2003); Rodger Shanahan and others on SCIRI and Daʿwa.

entries.label: Documenting the crimes
entries.hint: The evidentiary record of the regime's crimes was assembled as they happened and after: Middle East Watch's investigation of the Anfal, complete with satellite images and survivor testimony; the eighteen tonnes of captured Baʿth secret-police files seized in the north in 1991 and shipped to the United States; and, once the regime fell, the forensic teams at the mass graves. It became the basis of the later trials.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Genocide in Iraq: The Anfal Campaign' (1993); Kanan Makiya on the Iraq Memory Foundation and the Baʿth archive.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The war economy and the debt, the Kuwait grievance and the invasion, the sanctions and the collapse, Oil-for-Food and the siege economy, and the wrecked environment and resource base

entries.label: The war economy and the debt
entries.hint: The Iran war was paid for by running down Iraq's reserves and by loans and grants from the Gulf states — perhaps forty to eighty billion dollars from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia alone. The whole economy was bent to the front, arms were bought on credit from a dozen suppliers, and a war-contracting class grew rich. Iraq ended the war with the region's largest army and a debt it could not service.
entries.note: Abbas Alnasrawi, 'The Economy of Iraq' (1994); Kiren Aziz Chaudhry, 'The Price of Wealth' (1997).

entries.label: The Kuwait grievance and the invasion
entries.hint: By 1990 Saddam wanted Kuwait to forgive the war debt and pay reparations, to cut its oil output to lift the price, and to hand over two islands and the disputed end of the Rumaila field — which he accused it of draining by slant drilling. Kuwait refused. Reading Washington's signals as a green light, and needing money and a triumph, he took the whole country by force on 2 August.
entries.note: Lawrence Freedman & Efraim Karsh, 'The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991' (1993); the Glaspie transcript debate.

entries.label: The sanctions and the collapse
entries.hint: The comprehensive embargo of 1990, kept on after the war, cut Iraq off from selling its oil or buying almost anything. GDP fell by roughly three-quarters; the dinar collapsed from about three dollars to a fraction of a cent; savings and salaries were wiped out; skilled people fled or drove taxis; parts of the country reverted to barter. It was the fastest impoverishment of a modern middle-income state on record.
entries.note: Sarah Graham-Brown, 'Sanctioning Saddam' (1999); Abbas Alnasrawi, 'Iraq's Burdens: Oil, Sanctions, and Underdevelopment' (2002).

entries.label: Oil-for-Food and the siege economy
entries.hint: From 1996 the UN let Iraq sell a controlled amount of oil to buy food and medicine under UN supervision. It kept people alive and pulled the economy back from the abyss, and it leaked money to the regime everywhere — the surcharges on the oil, the kickbacks on the contracts, the vouchers handed to friendly politicians and journalists abroad. A rationed, monitored, corrupt economy of scarcity, run for seven years.
entries.note: the Independent Inquiry Committee (Volcker Report) into the Oil-for-Food Programme (2005); Joy Gordon, 'Invisible War' (2010).

entries.label: The wrecked environment and resource base
entries.hint: Twenty-four years of war and neglect left the physical country damaged for a generation: the marshes drained and their fishery gone, the irrigation and drainage systems decayed and the soil turning to salt, the date groves of the war zones cut down, the oil fields damaged and starved of parts. A country that had been feeding itself and exporting dates in 1979 was importing most of its food by 2003.
entries.note: the UNEP marshlands report (2001); the FAO and World Bank assessments of Iraqi agriculture in the 1990s.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The strategic-weapons programmes and their dismantlement, the military machine at its height and its decay, the infrastructure destroyed and jury-rigged, and the survival technologies of the sanctions years

entries.label: The strategic-weapons programmes and their dismantlement
entries.hint: By 1990 Iraq had the largest chemical-weapons programme since the Second World War, an advanced biological effort making anthrax and botulinum, extended-range Scud missiles, and a crash nuclear project that was months from a device. After the Gulf War the UN inspectorate and the IAEA dismantled almost all of it, destroying the stocks and the plants by the mid-1990s — a fact the regime obscured and the 2003 case for war ignored.
entries.note: the UNSCOM and UNMOVIC final reports; the Iraq Survey Group (Duelfer) Report (2004).

entries.label: The army at its height and its decay
entries.hint: In 1990 Iraq had the fourth-largest army in the world — a million men, the Republican Guard, a dense air-defence network. The Gulf War shattered the fielded force; then twelve years of sanctions rotted what remained, with no spare parts, no fuel for training and no new equipment. The army that met the 2003 invasion was a hollow shell, and it dissolved rather than fought.
entries.note: Anthony Cordesman, 'Iraq and the War of Sanctions' (1999); Kevin Woods & others, 'Iraqi Perspectives Project' (2006).

entries.label: The infrastructure destroyed and jury-rigged
entries.hint: The 1991 air campaign deliberately hit the electrical grid, the water-treatment plants and the telephone system; the sanctions then blocked the parts to fix them, on the grounds that pipes and pumps and chlorine had military uses. The result was chronic power cuts, contaminated water, and the return of cholera and typhoid to a country that had eradicated them. Iraqis kept the lights on with private generators and improvised repairs.
entries.note: the report by Thomas Nagy on the targeting of Iraqi water; Joy Gordon, 'Invisible War' (2010), on the 'dual-use' holds.

entries.label: The survival technologies of the sanctions years
entries.hint: A whole culture of ingenuity grew up around scarcity: the neighbourhood generator and the black-market fuel that ran it, the satellite dish smuggled in parts and assembled at night, the car kept alive for twenty years, the local workshops turning out spare parts and reconditioned medicines. Iraqis of the sanctions generation learned to fix anything, because nothing new could be bought.
entries.note: the ethnographic accounts of sanctions-era Baghdad; Nadje Al-Ali, 'Iraqi Women: Untold Stories from 1948 to the Present' (2007).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Iran war and the world's tilt toward Baghdad, from ally to pariah in 1990, the sanctions regime and the fracturing UN consensus, the Kurdish region and its four patrons, and 9/11 and the road to war

entries.label: The Iran war and the world's tilt
entries.hint: Once Iran took the initiative in 1982, the outside world lined up behind Iraq: American satellite intelligence and agricultural credits, French Mirages and Exocets, Soviet arms, Gulf money, European chemical-plant sales, and the US Navy escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers. Saddam was the barrier holding back Khomeini's revolution, and the gassing of Iranians and Kurds drew barely a protest. That indulgence ended abruptly in August 1990.
entries.note: Bruce Riedel, 'What We Won' background; Joost Hiltermann, 'A Poisonous Affair' (2007); the 'Iraqgate' investigations.

entries.label: From ally to pariah
entries.hint: The invasion of Kuwait reversed everything overnight. The Security Council condemned it within hours and imposed total sanctions within four days; thirty-five states, including Arab ones and the Soviet Union, joined a coalition; the UN authorised the use of force. It was the largest and broadest military alliance since the Second World War, and Iraq went from Western client to international outlaw in a fortnight.
entries.note: Lawrence Freedman & Efraim Karsh, 'The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991' (1993).

entries.label: The sanctions regime and the fracturing consensus
entries.hint: The Security Council kept Iraq under the most comprehensive sanctions in its history, tied to disarmament that the inspectors largely completed by the mid-1990s. As the humanitarian toll mounted, the consensus cracked: the United States and Britain held the hardest line, France, Russia and China pushed to ease it, the humanitarian exemptions never sufficed, and the Oil-for-Food corruption discredited the whole apparatus.
entries.note: David Malone, 'The International Struggle Over Iraq: Politics in the UN Security Council 1980–2005' (2006).

entries.label: The Kurdish region and its four patrons
entries.hint: The Kurdish safe haven survived on the sufferance of others: American, British and French aircraft flying the no-fly zone; Turkey allowing the operation from Incirlik while sending its own army in against the PKK using the same space; Iran backing the PUK; the KDP leaning on Turkey and, briefly in 1996, calling in Saddam's tanks against its Kurdish rival. It was a protectorate with four masters and no formal status.
entries.note: David McDowall, 'A Modern History of the Kurds' (2004); Michael Gunter, 'The Kurdish Predicament in Iraq' (1999).

entries.label: 9/11 and the road to war
entries.hint: The attacks of 11 September 2001 turned an argument into a plan. The administration pivoted from Afghanistan to Iraq, asserted a link to al-Qaeda that did not exist and a reconstituted weapons programme that did not exist, took a demand for disarmament to the UN in resolution 1441, failed to win a second resolution, assembled a 'coalition of the willing', and invaded on 20 March 2003.
entries.note: the report of the Iraq Inquiry (Chilcot Report, 2016); the US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence reports on prewar assessments.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The self-inflicted catastrophe, the three wars and the genocide, the unmaking of Iraqi society, and the fall of 2003 as a beginning not an end

entries.label: The self-inflicted catastrophe
entries.hint: In 1979 Iraq was a middle-income, fast-developing, secular Arab state with the best schools and hospitals in the region and a large modern middle class. Twenty-four years later, after three wars and thirteen of siege that its own ruler had chosen, it was among the poorest, most damaged and most traumatised countries on earth. It is the largest single reversal of human development in the modern record.
entries.note: the UNDP Iraq Living Conditions Survey (2004); Abbas Alnasrawi, 'Iraq's Burdens' (2002).

entries.label: Three wars and a genocide
entries.hint: The war with Iran, the Anfal against the Kurds, the invasion of Kuwait and the Gulf War, and the massacres of 1991: by the choices of one man, perhaps a million and a half Iraqis and Iranians died in a decade, and a society was soaked in violence, fear and grief. The habit of mass killing as an instrument of policy, and of enduring it in silence, was learned in these years.
entries.note: the casualty estimates compiled in Pierre Razoux (2015) and Human Rights Watch (1993).

entries.label: The unmaking of Iraqi society
entries.hint: The sanctions decade destroyed the middle class, emptied the professions through exile, restored the tribes, re-Islamised the streets, sharpened every line of sect and ethnicity, and made brutality and the black market normal. When the regime fell in 2003 it removed the lid from a society that had already been coming apart underneath for a dozen years. The chaos that followed had deep roots.
entries.note: Fanar Haddad, 'Sectarianism in Iraq' (2011); Toby Dodge, 'Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism' (2012).

entries.label: 2003 — the fall as a beginning
entries.hint: The Baʿth and Saddam were gone in three weeks. But the invasion removed a regime without a plan for what came next, into a country deformed by twenty-four years of tyranny and thirteen of siege, with its army dissolved, its state gutted, its society armed and angry and divided. The war was the shortest chapter of Iraq's ordeal. The occupation, the insurgency and the sectarian war were still ahead.
entries.note: George Packer, 'The Assassins' Gate' (2005); Ali Allawi, 'The Occupation of Iraq' (2007).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Saddam Hussein, Ali Hassan al-Majid, Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr, the Iraqi in exile, and the child of the sanctions

entries.label: Saddam Hussein
entries.hint: In twenty-four years as president he started three wars, used poison gas on Iranians and on his own Kurdish citizens, annexed a neighbour, defied the world through a decade of siege, and reduced the richest Arab country to penury while raising forty palaces. Pulled from a hole near Tikrit in December 2003, tried by an Iraqi court, and hanged on the first morning of Eid al-Adha in December 2006, taunting his executioners.
entries.note: Con Coughlin, 'Saddam: The Secret Life' (2002); the transcript of the Dujail trial.

entries.label: Ali Hassan al-Majid
entries.hint: Saddam's cousin, known to the Kurds as 'Chemical Ali'. He ran the Anfal campaign, signed the orders for the gas attacks, governed occupied Kuwait, and directed the crushing of the south in 1991. He was captured in 2003, convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity in four separate trials, and executed in January 2010 — the archetype of the regime's enforcer, a man who did the killing that the leader ordered.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Genocide in Iraq' (1993); the Anfal trial record of the Iraqi High Tribunal.

entries.label: Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr
entries.hint: The 'second Sadr', a cousin of the executed Muhammad Baqir, who from the mid-1990s did what no one else dared — preached openly, held mass Friday prayers, built a following among the poor Shia of Baghdad's slums and the southern towns, all under the regime's watch. In February 1999 he was shot dead in his car in Najaf with two of his sons. His third son, Muqtada, would turn the movement he left into a militia and a political bloc.
entries.note: Patrick Cockburn, 'Muqtada: Muqtada al-Sadr, the Shia Revival, and the Struggle for Iraq' (2008).

entries.label: The Iraqi in exile
entries.hint: A doctor, an engineer, a professor, a poet — someone who left in the 1980s or 1990s for Amman or Abu Dhabi or London or Detroit or Sydney, joining a diaspora of two to four million. They kept a parallel Iraq alive — the money sent home, the political fronts, the presses, the arguments — and watched from outside as the country they had left was ground down. A handful returned in 2003 to run it. Most did not.
entries.note: Nadje Al-Ali, 'Iraqi Women' (2007); the diaspora literature and the returnee memoirs.

entries.label: The child of the sanctions
entries.hint: Born around 1990 in Baghdad or Basra, growing up with the ration card, the power cuts, the water you had to boil, and a school with no glass in the windows and no paper for the books; probably underweight, possibly stunted; knowing the war and the siege as the only conditions of life. The generation that came of age in 2003 — into an occupation, an insurgency, and a country whose institutions and economy had already been hollowed out.
entries.note: the UNICEF Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys of Iraq (1996, 2000); Nadje Al-Ali & Nicola Pratt, 'What Kind of Liberation?' (2009).
